blocks.text: Paul later describes his use of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory, mapping women, sons, mountains, covenants, and Jerusalems within a polemical argument. His construction is relevant to discussions of this opening verse, but its details remain contested.

The chapter closes by calling this promise the heritage of the servants of Jehovah, using a plural term. Elsewhere in Isaiah, servant language can refer to Jacob or Israel and to a plural community, while singular servant poems have prompted differing identifications. This makes it important not to assume that every use of “servant” in Isaiah has the same referent.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings show that the book was actively copied and interpreted.

sections.title: The Book of Isaiah in Transmission
